blocks.x: In Ki Aikido (a style of Aikido that I train in and help teach), many techniques have two roles: the one performing the technique (nage) and the one attacking and being thrown (uke). The word “uke” actually is a form of the verb “ukeru”, meaning “to receive”, and you can think of this as literally “receiving” the technique applied by the nage. How one receives the technique, including rolling or falling, is called “ukemi”. (The “mi” part means “body” 身, which happens to be the same “mi” from “sashimi”.)

The ideal ukemi is light, in the sense that the person being thrown feels as if they are physically lightweight and moves smoothly where they are led, as opposed to being a heavy lump that just sits there without responding. This is especially so when showing a demonstration with a sensei in front of students, since light ukemi is often able to better showcase the nage’s throwing.

Personally I have been told several times by upper level senseis that my ukemi is too heavy and I should endeavor to make it lighter, so this is something I’ve thought about a good bit. Hence my writing this article about what really makes ukemi light.

There are a few factors in what makes ukemi feel “light”, and I want to go over them. As with most of my articles on Ki Aikido, this reflects my own experiences and opinions, and nothing official or canon. Still, I hope it helps others in their (Ki) Aikido journey.

One of the factors is how physically heavy and large the uke is. This is one that isn’t discussed much, but I think it is a factor. Physical abilities and techniques aside, the people I’ve worked with who have ukemi definitely tend to be a bit on the smaller or lighter side.

Having said that, I think there is a lot an uke can do to feel lighter, though some of it is not obvious at first. For a waza where a grab is required (like katate-tori where uke grabs nage’s wrist), holding lightly, yet in a connected/wrapping way that we call “holding with ki”, can go a long way to making things feel light. However, the tricky part is when nage begins to lead uke around on the mat, sometimes in a forward direction (zenpou nage) or in a spiral down towards the mat (many tenkan wazas do this).

The trick is to maintain the light (yet connected) feeling while moving. This requires the uke keeping up with the nage as they are led, without getting behind. Keeping up requires physically being able to move fast enough so that uke’s posture doesn’t break, which requires physical agility/speed. But an important part of light ukemi is being able to move quickly without making a lot of noise pounding the mat with your feet. It’s a bit hard to describe how to do this in words, but if you pay attention to the sound your feet make you can do trial-and-error to improve it over time.

Being able to accurately follow the nage’s leads also requires quick physical response on the uke’s side. Each person has physical limitations here, but “extending ki” and “keeping one point” generally help out. The uke can also think of being in the present moment, and calmly observing the nage to see where they are leading (sometimes even before they lead) and “ride on their ki”.

Doing light ukemi where the nage spins the uke towards the ground in a spiral-like pattern is particularly difficult to master. There are two tricks to help this. One is for the uke to tilt his or her body so that their legs are farther away, and head closer. I want to clarify that this doesn’t mean you bend your back or legs in a strange way, rather you tilt your entire body at an angle while maintaining good posture. The second trick is sort of a corollary to the first: walk a wide circle around. Even though this means moving your legs across more space, it’s somehow easier and gives you more control as you go around. These things can be quite awkward when you first try them, but practice makes better.

Remember performing a two-person waza is a two-way street. If the nage doesn’t lead in an effective way, the nage may have trouble following naturally. For example, even the best, most lightest ukes have a physical limitation after which they cannot follow smoothly, so it is the nage’s responsibility to figure out that line and adjust accordingly. On the other hand, leading slightly faster than the uke can smoothly follow can help the uke develop their speed and agility and take things to the next level, though it depends on the individual and where they are on their training path.

Another factor of light ukemi is how the uke interacts with the mat when falling or rolling. The uke should try to make as little noise as possible, though if they are thrown hard that can make some sound hard to avoid. Again, being aware of the sound you make can be used along with trial-and-error to make things quieter. You can also record yourself to hear how loud you smack the mat, and see what part of your body is doing it.

Finally, I want to emphasize that knowing the “right” type of ukemi depends on the situation. For example, if you are training at a high level it is not uncommon to “hold back” a little instead of going with the flow regardless of what the nage does. This can help the nage to throw more effectively and with more Ki. “Hold back” doesn’t mean to actively pull away from them and fight, however. Instead, it is about “keeping weight underside” and staying in one place unless you are effectively led somewhere else.
If you want to read another article on ukemi, check out this on “touchless” Aikido: https://selftaughtjapanese.com/2026/09/22/touchless-throwing-in-aikido/
